name: TMJ Botox

lead: TMJ Botox refers to injecting botulinum toxin into jaw muscles, such as the masseter or lateral pterygoid, to calm overactive muscles in people with temporomandibular disorders or teeth grinding. Users also seek it for a slimmer, softer lower face, since weakening the masseter reduces its bulk, and for more even jaw muscles.

Botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at nerve endings, temporarily weakening the injected muscle. In TMD the rationale is that lateral pterygoid spasm may contribute to anterior disc displacement. Multiple randomized trials of lateral pterygoid injection report benefit, while a set of newer registered trials is small and results are mixed in the sources.

paras: A clinician injects the muscles in a short visit, and it is a prescription treatment. Effects typically last months, so people repeat it periodically, with changes building over a few weeks.

Toxin spread can cause a fixed facial expression that resolves as the effect wears off. Use for TMD is generally off-label. Pregnant or breastfeeding people and those with certain neuromuscular conditions are commonly advised to avoid it.

Overview of Botulinum Toxins for Aesthetic Uses

angle.text: Botulinum toxin in the jaw muscles is used for clenching and jaw pain, and users also seek it for a slimmer lower face or more even jaw muscles as the treated masseter shrinks. Facial slimming is a recognized effect of treating the masseter, and the symmetry use is off-label.

lead: TMJ Botox is the use of botulinum toxin injections in the jaw muscles, chiefly the masseter, temporalis and lateral pterygoid, to treat temporomandibular joint disorders (TMD), bruxism (clenching and grinding) and related jaw pain. It is performed by clinicians and is a prescription treatment.[1]

Because the masseter is the thick muscle at the angle of the jaw, weakening it also changes the lower face: a 2019 literature review of the masseter in facial contouring reports that botulinum toxin reduces muscle bulk and reshapes the lower face while also improving pain and clenching symptoms.[2] This is why jaw Botox appears both in dental and TMD practice and in aesthetic clinics as a way to slim a wide or square lower face.[3]

According to Wikipedia, injection into the lateral pterygoid muscle has been studied in multiple randomized trials with evidence of benefit for TMD, and effects typically last months. The theory behind the approach is that spasm of this muscle contributes to anterior disc displacement.[1] Numerous trials are also registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, including small recently completed studies; the registry entries do not report outcomes.
infobox: Effects typically last two to four months in cosmetic use [15]
Botox first FDA-approved for strabismus and blepharospasm in 1989; cosmetic glabellar lines 2002 [15]

sections.h: Background: TMD and the jaw muscles
paras: Wikipedia describes TMD as a spectrum of disorders of the muscles of mastication and the temporomandibular joints, with pain, restricted jaw movement and joint noises as the main symptoms; it reports a global prevalence of 34 percent, highest in South America (47 percent) and lowest in North America (26 percent).[1] There is no single accepted treatment protocol, and common treatments include occlusal splints, cognitive behavioural therapy, physical therapy and pain medication.[1]

The muscles that raise the jaw are the masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid, while the lateral pterygoid helps move the jaw forward and sideways; a theory discussed in TMD literature holds that the lower head of the lateral pterygoid contracts when it should relax in people with anterior disc displacement, which motivates injecting it.[1] Bruxism and TMD co-occur in some people, although the relationship is debated.[1]

Investigators have registered trials of botulinum toxin for TMD with bruxism, anterior disc displacement, myofascial pain, TMJ dislocation and scleroderma-related restriction of mouth opening.[4][5][6][7][8][9][10]
Registered trials also compare toxin with other treatments, including arthrocentesis, splints, acupuncture and dry needling.[6][11][12][13]

Aesthetic reviews describe botulinum toxin injection of the masseter as a treatment for masseter muscle hypertrophy, an enlarged muscle that makes the lower face look broad.[2][14][3] Wikipedia notes that injecting the masseter can reduce chewing power for solid foods and that the toxin is used to relax jaw clenching.[15]

A 36-article review of adverse events after masseter injections reports that complications typically appear 2 to 4 weeks after injection and resolve within 12 weeks.[14] The 2019 review describes adverse effects as minimal and short-lasting.[2]
Wikipedia's TMD article states that lateral pterygoid injection has been examined in multiple randomized trials with evidence of benefit.[1]

ClinicalTrials.gov registrations include: a Phase 1 study of Botox for TMD with bruxism that was withdrawn (NCT02202070);[4] a completed 10-patient study of ultrasound-guided toxin injection for disc displacement with reduction (NCT07076355);[5] a completed 39-patient study combining i-PRF after arthrocentesis with lateral pterygoid Botox (NCT06207955);[7] a completed Phase 2/3 study of 20 patients with bilateral TMD (NCT05651256);[10] a completed 17-patient early-phase study in scleroderma (NCT04523506);[8] a randomized trial comparing arthrocentesis with toxin (NCT07736521) not yet recruiting;[6] and a 60-person study of splint, toxin, or medication plus splint care for clenching and jaw symptoms (NCT07586072).[13] Other registered studies compare a mandibular splint with toxin and compare acupuncture, dry needling and toxin.[11][12] Results are not posted in the registry entries.
Reviews of the aesthetic use describe lower-face reshaping and muscle-bulk reduction after masseter injection, and the registered TMD studies listed here do not measure appearance outcomes.[2][3]
Wikipedia describes a general lack of evidence for any single TMD treatment and lists occlusal splints, psychosocial interventions, physical therapy and pain medication among common approaches.[1]
A reported complication is a fixed facial expression from toxin diffusing to nearby muscles, which resolves as the effect wears off.[1]

In the broader botulinum toxin literature, most cosmetic side effects come from unintended weakness of nearby facial muscles, bruising, headaches and flu-like symptoms; the FDA warned in 2008 and added boxed warnings in 2009 about spread of the toxin from the injection site, and high continued doses can cause muscle atrophy that is described as recovering after a break.[15]

In appearance-focused circles the treatment is discussed as a way to calm hyperactive jaw muscles and slim the lower face. Published reviews of masseter injection describe that contouring effect, while the TMD trials focus on pain and disc outcomes.[2][3]

Alan B. Scott tested botulinum toxin in monkey eye muscles and injected the first strabismus patients in 1977, naming the drug Oculinum; the FDA approved it for adult strabismus and blepharospasm in 1989, after which Allergan adopted the Botox trademark, and Botox Cosmetic was approved for glabellar lines in 2002.[15]

timeline.event: Alan B. Scott injects the first strabismus patients with botulinum toxin.[15]
FDA approves Oculinum (later Botox) for strabismus and blepharospasm.[15]
FDA approves Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines.[15]
FDA adds boxed warnings about distant spread of toxin.[15]
